title: The Atmosphere and Weather
seo_title: Earth Sciences 11: The Atmosphere and Weather Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
short_title: atmospheric circulation, air masses and fronts
standard_text: The transfer of energy through the atmosphere creates weather: layers of the atmosphere, global circulation, air masses, fronts and pressure systems, and weather data. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Earth Sciences 11)
meta_desc: Free Earth Sciences 11 worksheets (BC Curriculum): atmospheric circulation, air masses and fronts. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Uneven heating of Earth drives the winds.
key_sub: Warm air rises; cold air sinks.
body_html:
How to think about it

The atmosphere has layers: troposphere (weather), stratosphere (ozone), mesosphere and thermosphere. The Sun heats the equator more than the poles; this uneven heating and Earth's rotation (the Coriolis effect) create global wind belts and circulation cells.

Air masses take on the temperature and moisture of where they form. A front is the boundary between two air masses: cold fronts bring short, heavy showers; warm fronts bring longer, gentler rain. Low pressure brings clouds and rain; high pressure brings clear skies.

Example

In which layer of the atmosphere does weather happen?

The lowest layer

Answer: the troposphere

Example

Air rises over the Coast Mountains. What happens on the windward side?

Rising air cools.

Answer: clouds and heavy rain

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up weather and climate.
  • Thinking high pressure brings storms.
  • Forgetting Earth's rotation in wind direction.

faq.q: Why is the Okanagan drier than Vancouver?
faq.a: It is in the rain shadow of the Coast Mountains.
A warming of the eastern Pacific that changes weather patterns, often giving BC milder winters.

items.q: Which part of the water cycle returns most water from land to the atmosphere in a forest?
items.e: Trees release water vapour through their leaves.

items.q: What are the trade winds?
c: winds that blow only at night
steady easterly winds blowing towards the Equator from about 30° latitude
items.e: In the Southern Hemisphere they are south-easterlies.

items.q: What is the enhanced greenhouse effect?
c: extra warming caused by greenhouse gases added by human activity
the warming caused by the Sun getting hotter
the natural warming that keeps Earth habitable
items.e: CO₂ from fossil fuels is the main cause.

items.q: What is a Hadley cell?
c: a circulation in which warm air rises near the Equator and sinks near 30° latitude
an ocean current along the Equator
items.e: There are Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells.

items.q: What is upwelling?
c: cold, nutrient-rich deep water rising to the surface
items.e: Upwelling areas are very productive fisheries.

items.q: Which way does air circulate around a high-pressure system in the Southern Hemisphere?
items.e: Highs bring stable, dry weather.

items.q: What is latent heat's role in weather?
c: energy taken up in evaporation is released when water vapour condenses in clouds, powering storms
items.e: Tropical cyclones are fuelled by latent heat.

items.q: What happens to the surplus of energy at the tropics?
c: winds and ocean currents carry it towards the poles
it is stored in the core
it is lost into space at once
items.e: This drives global circulation.

items.q: Why is the stratosphere warmer at the top than at the bottom?
c: ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the Sun
the air is denser at the top
it is closer to Earth's core
items.e: In the troposphere temperature falls with height.

items.q: How does heat move through the mantle?
c: mostly by convection: hot rock slowly rises and cooler rock sinks
items.e: Convection takes millions of years.

items.q: What is evaporation in the water cycle?
c: liquid water changing to water vapour, using energy from the Sun
items.e: Most evaporation is from the oceans.

items.q: Why does the land heat up faster than the sea?
c: land has a higher specific heat capacity
water has a higher specific heat capacity and mixes, so the sea warms more slowly
items.e: This causes sea breezes.

items.q: What does a tropical cyclone need to form?
c: warm sea water (above about 26.5 °C), moist air and enough Coriolis effect
items.e: Cyclones weaken over land or cold water.

items.q: What is the global conveyor belt?
c: the worldwide thermohaline circulation linking all the oceans
items.e: A full circuit may take about 1000 years.

items.q: Why does the Equator receive more solar energy per square metre than the poles?
c: it is closer to the Sun
sunlight hits it more directly, so the energy is spread over a smaller area
items.e: At the poles the same beam is spread out.

items.q: What is an aquifer?
c: a layer of porous, permeable rock that holds and transmits groundwater
items.e: Sandstone is often a good aquifer.

items.q: Why are tropical cyclones not found near the Equator?
c: the Coriolis effect is too weak there to make the air spin
the ocean is too cold there
items.e: Cyclones form between about 5° and 20° latitude.

items.q: What is the main store of fresh water on Earth?
items.e: About 69% of fresh water is ice.

items.q: How does the greenhouse effect work?
c: greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation from Earth's surface and re-emit some back down
items.e: Without it Earth would average about −18 °C.

items.q: What happens to the solar radiation that reaches Earth?
c: it is all absorbed by the Moon
some is reflected, some is absorbed by the atmosphere and most is absorbed by the surface
it all passes back into space unchanged
items.e: Absorbed energy is later emitted as infrared.

items.q: Emma's forecast says a cold front is coming. What weather should Emma expect?
c: Thunderstorms or heavy rain, then cooler and drier weather.
Light, steady rain or drizzle, then warmer and more humid weather.
Many days of cloudy, wet weather.
items.e: A cold air mass pushes under a warm air mass and forces it up quickly.

items.q: Leah's forecast says an occluded front is coming. What weather should Leah expect?
c: Thunderstorms or heavy rain, then cooler and drier weather.
Light, steady rain or drizzle, then warmer and more humid weather.
Many days of cloudy, wet weather.
items.e: A cold front catches up to a warm front and lifts the warm air off the ground.

items.q: Chloe reads about a cold and dry air mass. Where did it most likely form?
items.e: A continental polar air mass forms over cold land far north.

items.q: Nathan learns that an air mass formed over northern Canada. What will it most likely be like?
items.e: Air masses take on the temperature and humidity of where they form: over cold land far north.

items.q: Benjamin reads: “Two air masses meet but neither moves much.” What kind of front is this?
items.e: That describes a stationary front.

items.q: Kai reads about a warm and humid air mass. Where did it most likely form?
items.e: A maritime tropical air mass forms over warm ocean water near the equator.

items.q: Chloe's forecast says a warm front is coming. What weather should Chloe expect?
c: Light, steady rain or drizzle, then warmer and more humid weather.
Thunderstorms or heavy rain, then cooler and drier weather.
Many days of cloudy, wet weather.
items.e: A warm air mass slides up over a cold air mass.

items.q: Noah reads: “A cold air mass pushes under a warm air mass and forces it up quickly.” What kind of front is this?
items.e: That describes a cold front.

items.q: Chloe reads about a cool and humid air mass. Where did it most likely form?
items.e: A maritime polar air mass forms over cold ocean water.

items.q: Aiden learns that an air mass formed over the North Pacific. What will it most likely be like?
items.e: Air masses take on the temperature and humidity of where they form: over cold ocean water.

items.q: Hana reads about a cool and humid air mass. Where did it most likely form?
items.e: A maritime polar air mass forms over cold ocean water.

items.q: Ethan learns that an air mass formed over the cold North Atlantic. What will it most likely be like?
items.e: Air masses take on the temperature and humidity of where they form: over cold ocean water.

items.q: Emma reads: “A warm air mass slides up over a cold air mass.” What kind of front is this?
items.e: That describes a warm front.

items.q: Ethan learns that an air mass formed over the Gulf of Mexico. What will it most likely be like?
items.e: Air masses take on the temperature and humidity of where they form: over warm ocean water near the equator.

items.q: Hana learns that an air mass formed over central Canada in winter. What will it most likely be like?
items.e: Air masses take on the temperature and humidity of where they form: over cold land far north.

items.q: Ethan's forecast says a stationary front is coming. What weather should Ethan expect?
c: Light, steady rain or drizzle, then warmer and more humid weather.
Many days of cloudy, wet weather.
Thunderstorms or heavy rain, then cooler and drier weather.
items.e: Two air masses meet but neither moves much.

items.q: Zoe reads about a warm and humid air mass. Where did it most likely form?
items.e: A maritime tropical air mass forms over warm ocean water near the equator.

items.q: Zoe reads about a cold and dry air mass. Where did it most likely form?
items.e: A continental polar air mass forms over cold land far north.

items.q: Chloe learns that an air mass formed over the deserts of northern Mexico. What will it most likely be like?
items.e: Air masses take on the temperature and humidity of where they form: over hot, dry land.

items.q: Zoe reads about a hot and dry air mass. Where did it most likely form?
items.e: A continental tropical air mass forms over hot, dry land.

items.q: What does a barometer measure?
items.e: Changes in pressure help forecast weather.

items.q: Ava's weather station records a drop from 25 °C to 14 °C in two hours with a wind shift. What most likely happened?
items.e: A sharp temperature drop is a sign of a cold front.

items.q: What causes air masses to move?
c: winds and differences in air pressure
items.e: Air moves from high to low pressure.

items.q: Why does weather in most of the United States usually move from west to east?
c: The prevailing winds (westerlies) carry air masses east.
items.e: Forecasters look west to see what is coming.

items.q: Chloe wants to forecast tomorrow's weather. Which data would help most?
c: the air masses and fronts moving toward her town from the west
the weather in her town last year
the colour of the sky at noon only
items.e: Weather moves; look at what is coming.

items.q: Which air mass would bring warm, humid weather to the southeastern United States?
c: cold air from the North Pacific
maritime tropical air from the Gulf of Mexico
items.e: Maritime = ocean (humid), tropical = warm.

items.q: After a cold front passes, the weather usually becomes
items.e: Cold, dry air replaces warm, moist air.

items.q: Chloe's barometer reading has been falling all morning. What does this suggest?
c: Stormy or rainy weather may be coming.
items.e: Falling pressure often means a low-pressure system is arriving.

items.q: A meteorologist sees a cold air mass moving toward warm, humid air. What should she warn people about?
c: possible thunderstorms as the front passes
items.e: Cold fronts can bring strong storms.

items.q: Why are humid summer days followed by cooler days after a storm?
c: A cold, dry air mass moved in behind a cold front.
items.e: New air masses change the weather.

items.q: What is an air mass?
c: a huge body of air with about the same temperature and humidity throughout
items.e: Air masses can cover thousands of kilometres.

items.q: What is a front?
c: the boundary where two different air masses meet
items.e: Weather often changes at fronts.

items.q: Noah sees a big L (low pressure) over the town on the weather map. What weather is likely?
c: dry, calm weather for a week
items.e: Rising air in a low-pressure area cools and forms clouds.

items.q: Benjamin sees thin, high clouds, then thicker, lower clouds and light rain over a day, and then it gets warmer. What is this pattern?
c: a stationary front lasting a week
items.e: Warm fronts bring gradual changes and light rain.

items.q: Hana sees a big H (high pressure) over the town on the weather map. What weather is likely?
items.e: Sinking air in a high-pressure area keeps clouds from forming.

items.e: The temperature fell from 26 °C to 17 °C after the thunderstorm.

items.q: Why do cold fronts often bring thunderstorms?
c: Warm, moist air is pushed up quickly, cools and forms tall clouds.
items.e: Fast-rising air builds storm clouds.

items.q: Sofia's barometer reading has been rising after a storm. What does this suggest?
items.e: Rising pressure often means a high-pressure system is arriving.

c: They all get the same rain.

items.q: Sofia studies the Gulf Stream, a warm current. How does it affect climate?
c: It makes the coast of Newfoundland cold and foggy.
It brings warmer water and milder weather to southern Japan.
It makes Western Europe warmer than other places that far north.
It makes the coast of Peru and Chile cool and dry.
items.e: The Gulf Stream makes Western Europe warmer than other places that far north.

items.q: Hana reads that the Humboldt Current flows north along the west coast of South America. Is it a warm or a cold current?
c: a current of air, not water
items.e: Currents that flow from near the equator toward the poles are warm; currents from the poles are cold.

items.q: Leah reads that the Labrador Current flows south from the Arctic along the coast of Canada. Is it a warm or a cold current?
c: a current of air, not water
items.e: Currents that flow from near the equator toward the poles are warm; currents from the poles are cold.

items.q: Maya completes the sentence: “Air near the ground ____.”
c: rises, because it is less dense
sinks, because it is more dense
moves from high pressure toward low pressure
items.e: Air near the ground moves from high pressure toward low pressure.

items.q: Ethan completes the sentence: “Cold air at the poles ____.”
c: sinks, because it is more dense
curve to the right because Earth rotates
rises, because it is less dense
moves from high pressure toward low pressure
items.e: Cold air at the poles sinks, because it is more dense.

items.q: How do warm ocean currents affect nearby land?
c: They make the climate warmer and often wetter.
items.e: The ocean shares its heat with the air.

items.q: What does unequal heating of Earth cause?
c: air and water to move, creating winds and ocean currents
items.e: Heat differences drive circulation.

items.q: Emma compares Seattle (west of the Cascade Mountains) and Yakima (east of the Cascades). Which gets more rain?
items.e: Moist ocean air rises over the mountains and drops rain on the west side; the east side is in a rain shadow.

items.q: Leah completes the sentence: “Warm air at the equator ____.”
c: moves in a straight line no matter what
rises, because it is less dense
curve to the right because Earth rotates
sinks, because it is more dense
items.e: Warm air at the equator rises, because it is less dense.

items.q: Zoe asks why the equator is the warmest part of Earth on average. What is the best explanation?
c: Sunlight hits the equator at the most direct angle, so the energy is concentrated in a small area.
The moon heats the equator more.
There is more ocean at the equator.
The equator is closer to the sun.
items.e: Unequal heating comes from the angle of sunlight, not the distance to the sun.

items.q: Hana completes the sentence: “Winds in the Northern Hemisphere ____.”
c: sinks, because it is more dense
moves in a straight line no matter what
rises, because it is less dense
curve to the right because Earth rotates
items.e: Winds in the Northern Hemisphere curve to the right because Earth rotates.

items.q: What is a rain shadow?
c: a dry area on the side of a mountain away from the ocean wind
items.e: Air drops its rain on the windward side.

items.q: Why does the equator get more energy from the sun than the poles?
c: Sunlight hits the equator more directly, so the energy is concentrated.
The poles are covered by clouds all the time.
The equator is closer to the sun.
items.e: The angle of sunlight causes unequal heating.

items.q: Lucas reads that the Kuroshio Current flows north along the coast of Japan. Is it a warm or a cold current?
c: a current of air, not water
items.e: Currents that flow from near the equator toward the poles are warm; currents from the poles are cold.

items.q: Why do coastal areas have milder temperatures than inland areas?
c: The ocean makes its own heat.
Water heats up and cools down more slowly than land.
items.e: Large bodies of water moderate climate.

items.q: Does warm air rise or sink?
c: rise, because it is less dense
items.e: Rising and sinking air form convection cells.

items.q: Emma compares San Francisco (on the coast) and Sacramento (inland). Which has a smaller difference between summer and winter temperatures?
items.e: The ocean warms and cools slowly, so coastal places have milder temperatures.

items.q: Jayden asks why the poles are the coldest parts of Earth. What is the best explanation?
c: The poles never get any sunlight.
Sunlight hits the poles at a slant, so the energy is spread over a large area.
The poles are much farther from the sun.
items.e: Slanted sunlight spreads the same energy over more area.

Which surface has the lowest albedo?
items.e: Dark surfaces absorb most sunlight.
